#10595. Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10592. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10590. A grand new start of it: Exploring Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s effect on business—in New York City and beyond

A democratic socialist running the financial capital of the universe? For a magazine obsessed with how business can change—and change the world—it’s hard to imagine a more intriguing experiment.

As Zohran Mamdani wraps up his first year as New York City’s mayor, we decided to explore a possibility that got lost in the reductive shouting that surrounded his campaign: What if his democratic socialism-fueled agenda is actually good for business? And what will happen as other cities and states elect leaders with similar ideas?

Making New York more affordable is a goal that most of us can get behind. So is making city government faster, more responsive, and more innovative. The question—a thorny one—is whether Mamdani can deliver a more equitable city without throwing a wet blanket over the investment and entrepreneurship that help it thrive.

That tension animates this issue’s cover story, by Morgan Clendaniel, our executive editor, digital. Clendaniel, who has long covered the intersection of business and progressive politics, spoke to Tony Shorris, president and CEO of the NYC Economic Development Corporation, and Julie Su, deputy mayor for economic justice, about the sweeping role that they believe government can play in the economy—speeding up procurement, cutting red tape, making city services function.

The revolution may include city-owned grocery stores. It will definitely include high-tech public bathrooms.

Capitalism + democratic socialism

There’s something invigorating about that combination of grand ambition and attention to the daily details. At Fast Company, we spend a lot of time talking to visionaries who see a broken system and decide to build something better. It’s exciting to see that startup energy coursing through City Hall.

Clendaniel interviewed chief executives, too, such as Warby Parker’s Neil Blumenthal, and he spoke with key opposition figures, including Steven Fulop, president and CEO of the pro-business Partnership for New York City, and the venture capitalist Bradley Tusk. (Bill Ackman, the hedge fund manager, had his own words for the mayor at our Innovation Festival in September.)

This unfettered-capitalism crowd worries that the S-word alone is enough to discourage investment in New York and prompt companies to relocate or move jobs elsewhere. There’s some fearmongering here, no doubt, but also some merit. Business hates uncertainty.

These are complex questions worth exploring with an open mind and a willingness to scrutinize the trade-offs. Clendaniel does just that, with a big assist from his editor, Jill Bernstein.

A visual caffeine jolt

Meanwhile, our creative director, Mike Schnaidt, came up with the idea for the coffee cup on the cover, brought to life by illustrator Justin Metz. Along with Clendaniel and Bernstein’s journalism, this graphic effort reminds me why I love making this magazine. Even in the fully digitized, AI-ified year of 2026, a great magazine cover can turn a complicated argument into something immediate and surprising.

Here, an everyday New York object carries an extraordinary question about the future of the city—and the ever-evolving relationship between the private sector and the public good.

#10588. AI’s new business model: Break the internet, then sell the fix

People who work in cybersecurity or work on the fundamentals of digital infrastructure do not want to live in “exciting times,” but right now, they don’t have a choice.

Binance was just hacked in what is, so far, the largest cryptocurrency heist in history. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, narrowly averted a major attack through a third-party extension that would have allowed hackers to upload worms to the affected computers. A number of major airlines were affected when the Spanish travel-tech company Amadeus was hacked, leaking customer information on the web (mercifully without payment info, this time). At the center of this are generative AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which all at once are empowering hackers while billing themselves as the only line of defense. They’ve found a new niche, and it’s to become a protection racket. 

The threat is quantifiable: Severe bugs are classified as CVEs (common vulnerabilities and exposures), and around 400,000 have been officially logged since 1988. Of those, 13,000 happened in the last month. PHP2Shell is the perfect example of this. If you spent any time on social media in the last few weeks, you probably heard some chatter about PHP2Shell and just how dire the threat was. Roughly 70% of websites rely on code written using PHP, and the announcement of a fundamental bug in the language—akin to discovering that millions of buildings share the same faulty lock, potentially giving intruders easy access—had people panicking. Websites such as Wikimedia preemptively went offline until a fix was pushed through.

These bugs were rediscovered separately by two cybersecurity firms: Calif and Wiz. The bugs are very difficult to spot. They had to do with how the host computer accesses memory while an application is running: If a malicious actor forced an out of memory condition by whatever means, it would be possible to interrupt the runtime, leave a partially initialized object behind, and have the application treat it as valid. It would be a stepping stone for a hostile takeover of the host server, while a separate bug could leave instructions from a request that could be read again subsequently instead of being reset. This can be an apocalyptic threat if somebody can actually do those things. They would gain remote control over the host computer, and at that point they can do whatever they want with that machine and what’s on it.

Notably, developers at the PHP Foundation knew about this bug in 2024, but couldn’t agree on a solution for it. Every proposed fix had associated costs, and in any event, nobody actually knew how to act against these bugs. The threat was completely theoretical. It sat there, which wasn’t the optimal workflow, but it also wasn’t an omega-level threat until generative AI came into the picture. Forcing the condition while also creating the takeover wasn’t easy to do. Once the vulnerability was publicly announced, what had been a trickle of attacks became a flood. Fixes were rapidly pushed (in some cases by volunteers) and anybody running a website on PHP was urged to quickly upgrade to protect themselves.

This was just one bug, but pretty much everybody expects that more will be found. The people talking loudest about the danger are, surprisingly, generative artificial intelligence companies. AI companies are all too happy to make clear how incredibly dangerous all of this is and how many more bugs and vulnerabilities they expect to find as they continue to look around. Sam Altman doesn’t think we’ll be able to patch all the bugs, while Jason Clinton of Anthropic terms it a “vulnerability tsunami.” They’re promising years of instability following this as they struggle to discover and patch all of these bugs—an ongoing process, because software development is itself a process of continual updates. 

Why are they talking this way? They’re emphasizing how dangerous their product is, which seems like terrible salesmanship. But they’re also peddling the solution to the problem they helped to introduce.

And to force the issue, they’re going to look for the bugs themselves. That’s the point of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, which is all about looking for defects and vulnerabilities in open-source software. Nor are they just running around bug-hunting and letting chaos ensue. They’re trying to step into the cybersecurity space and set themselves up as the best solution to the problem.

OpenAI unveiled a new security-focused model in September, GPT-6 Cyber. OpenAI’s Daybreak program is intended to be available only to eligible organizations so that only “good actors” can take advantage of this, though in the long term as models become open access it’s not clear how that distinction will matter. Anthropic has its own model, Claude Mythos Preview. Google has Gemini Carbon 4 as its cybersecurity model. As with all models, you pay per token. Access to Daybreak is subsidized, although if you’re a believer in Cory Doctorow’s theory of enshittification, the long-term business model will be to make this more expensive over time as customers grow to depend on it. These companies are desperate for new sources of revenue even as overall revenue growth slows.

They’re not being subtle about this. Sam Altman told a group of business students at Stanford that “I think we’re going to have to completely switch the defense model to using the same technology for a new kind of defense shield.” In other words: Gotta use my products to keep yourself safe. What they’re doing verges on extortion; they’re trying to monetize the chaos their products are introducing. But in addition to that, they’re taking aim at a fundamentally vulnerable digital space.

A threat to the open-source commons

Let’s take a step back and consider how the internet, much of which runs on open-source software, is really maintained. PHP is supported by the PHP Foundation, which has just over a dozen employees and relies on donations. It is in effect a passion project for a few developers. There’s an Xkcd comic that sheds a great deal of light on this: Random critical pieces of digital infrastructure are being maintained by people entirely on their own, thanklessly and often without compensation. The modern open internet has been built up in ad hoc ways that often deprioritized security, but that mattered less when only human beings were doing the building or the hacking. To take advantage of those vulnerabilities would require not just expertise, but a great deal of time, effort, and computational power in many cases. PHP2Shell’s exploits were hard to spot, even if you really knew what you were doing and understood PHP down to the source code.

Yes, these potential threats are dire, but this isn’t a tsunami or a natural disaster that simply could not have been prevented. This is entirely manmade, and the people shrieking about what a dire emergency it is are also the ones who have helped to inaugurate it. This exploit sat virtually unknown by anybody for more than a decade, and even when it was recognized for what it was, the threat was purely theoretical. Now because of generative AI, cybersecurity is starting to favor the attack rather than the defender. People like Sam Altman helped to create the problem, first by developing the models, and now by going around and actively looking for weak points in our ramshackle internet. They broke it, and now they’re here to offer a solution: “Nice open internet you’ve got right there; it would be a shame if something happened to it.”

And what are the costs associated with this? For individual consumers of course, there’s the threat of hacks, theft, and general instability on the internet. For businesses, outages, lost revenue, and theft. That’s severe. But I think that there’s a more fundamental risk to the whole of the internet, at least as we know it. Groups like the PHP Foundation or the individual developers who sustain free and open-source software (FOSS) are going to be under even greater strain in the years to come, especially when compared to companies like Anthropic that, for the moment at least, have very deep pockets. Those 13,000 CVEs I mentioned at the beginning of the piece? Those largely fall on volunteers and overworked organizations to remediate, which will burn them out and in the long run likely push people away from the whole FOSS project. 

Turning to generative AI is probably what Anthropic and every other company wants, as another use case for their products, but it poses its own severe risks. Large language models (LLMs) are already being used on open-source projects that call into question the whole license-free structure and system of attribution that has made FOSS possible. That’s one leg of our stool that’s being kicked out from under us.

On top of that though, as AI-generated code winds up in more FOSS projects, is it going to introduce more vulnerabilities that will then have to be hunted down and eliminated? The answer seems to be yes. Whether it’s from vibe coding or simply the fact that LLMs trained on code with security vulnerabilities will tend to reproduce those vulnerabilities, we’re likely going to be running in place for years on end. And even if it can be introduced without undermining the security of the code itself, it’s another avenue to eat away at the licensure and copyright-free status that makes FOSS possible.

So this protection racket that’s forming is more than just a tax. It’s going to massively destabilize the ecosystem of the internet as we know it. I don’t know what comes next if the delicate FOSS sandbox falls apart. Maintainers could abandon their projects, which in turn creates more security vulnerabilities as things fall out of date and become obsolete. Even stably running pieces of infrastructure will eventually be unsupported by the languages that they run on; people can wake up one morning and find that some odd dependency powering their website stopped working. Who’s responsible at that point for fixing it? 

Nor do I want to see it entrusted to for-profit entities. Maintaining this work is basically thankless as it stands; it’s unprofitable to take on because the whole point is that everybody can freely use it. The only reason for them to do so in the long run would be to monetize it, which costs the rest of us. And as they make these into their own proprietary systems, will they wall off what is theirs from everything else? Why shouldn’t they; Microsoft spent years fighting the FOSS movement because it saw open-source software as a threat to its copyrighted systems. What has been up until now a true commons, maintained by people and organizations largely doing it out of passion, would become something else entirely: less able to talk to each other, and more expensive to use.

What’s the solution? This is probably a whole other essay, but in the long run it’s going to have to be government. Whether by directly assuming the burden or offering cash and resources to private groups, governments need to take steps to ensure that an open and free internet continues to exist. Could something like the United Nations do it, ensuring that it’s a truly global movement instead of under one national or regional umbrella? Failing that, could the European Union take it on—a prudent move, especially as Europe tries to get out from under the thumb of U.S. big tech. Food for thought, because under the shadow of all of these scary cyberattacks, that’s where I think the real threat lies.

#10585. How to Add AI Content Detection to Your Node.js App

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sooner or later someone on your team asks it. Maybe it’s a product manager, maybe the head of content, maybe a teacher who’s just marked forty near-identical essays: can we tell when people are pasting in ChatGPT output?

The short answer is no, not with certainty. Anyone who promises you that is selling something.

But you can get a useful signal, and you can show it to the people who actually make the call: editors, teachers, moderators. In this tutorial you’ll build a small Express app that takes some text, sends it to an AI detector API, waits for the result, and highlights the sentences that look machine-written.

I’m using the Quetext AI Detector API here. It scores each sentence, not just the whole document, and you can try it without a subscription. Most detection APIs follow the same submit, poll, fetch pattern, though. If you switch providers later, you’ll rewrite one file.

Put the key in an environment variable. Don’t hard-code it, and don’t let it anywhere near the browser.

You’ll make three calls. Analysis takes a few seconds, so the API hands you a ticket and makes you come back for the result. Keep the Quetext API docs open in another tab while you follow along; they list every endpoint, field and error code.

Every request sends your key in an X-API-Key header. The minimum input is 50 words, which sounds annoying until you realise no detector can say anything useful about a two-line comment.

And remember this number: 10 requests every 5 seconds, per account. Progress checks count. It’ll come back to bite you in the production section if you ignore it.

Create quetext.js. I like keeping everything provider-specific in one file, so the rest of the app has no idea who’s doing the detecting.

Three decisions in there that are worth a sentence each:

The errors keep their HTTP status code. A 402 means you’ve run out of credit and a 429 means you’re polling too fast, and you’ll want to handle those differently from “something broke.”

It polls every 2.5 seconds because Quetext’s docs suggest 2 to 3. Polling faster won’t speed the report up. You’ll just burn through the rate limit.

And there’s a hard timeout. Leave it out and one stuck report can hang a request forever. That’s a miserable bug to track down at 11pm.

Next, server.js. It checks the input, runs the three calls, and gives the frontend a simple response that doesn’t mention Quetext anywhere.

Look at the mapping at the end. generated_prob becomes probability, and ai_score comes back as a string like "82.50", so it gets parsed into a number. It’s a small detail. But it means your frontend never learns which provider’s field names it’s dealing with, and that’s what makes swapping providers a one-file change.

Show someone “64% AI” and they’ll jump to a conclusion. Show them a paragraph with three sentences shaded pink and they’ll actually read it.

So the page shows every sentence, coloured by how likely it is to be AI-generated. Create public/index.html:

Run node server.js and open http://localhost:3000. Try two samples: something you wrote yourself, then a raw chatbot answer on the same topic. Seeing which sentences light up teaches you more about how these detectors work than any diagram I could draw.

A quick security point. Those sentences came from your users, then went through an outside service. Treat them as untrusted. That’s why the code uses textContent and never innerHTML, as the OWASP XSS prevention cheat sheet recommends.

The demo keeps an HTTP request open while it polls. Fine on your laptop. Not fine with real traffic.

Submit the text, save the report id with a pending status, and respond straight away. A worker (BullMQ, a cron job, a serverless queue, whatever you already use) does the polling and updates the record once it’s done. The UI says “Checking…” until the result shows up.

Here’s how it goes wrong. It’s Monday morning, 20 editors open their review queues and click “Check” at roughly the same time. Each request polls on its own, and within a few seconds you’ve hit 429s across the board, because the 10-per-5-seconds limit covers your whole account, not each user.

Use one worker that loops through every pending report, with a short pause between calls. Problem solved.

You pay per word, so don’t check every blog comment. Article submissions, assignments and paid freelance work usually justify the cost. Cache results against a hash of the text too. Someone who submits the same draft three times shouldn’t cost you three times.

AI detection doesn’t catch copying. Someone can lift a 2019 blog post word for word and it’ll score 0% AI, because a human wrote it. Just not this human. If originality matters to your product, the same API has plagiarism endpoints that work exactly the same way. The API documentation covers both.

Developers skip this part. It’s also the part that ends up in angry support tickets.

In 2023, Liang and colleagues at Stanford ran essays written by non-native English speakers (all human, written for the TOEFL) through seven AI detectors. On average, the detectors labelled more than 61% of them as AI-generated. Simple vocabulary and textbook grammar read as “predictable,” and predictability is exactly what detectors look for.

Picture an international student getting an automatic zero because a script said so. You don’t want to be the person who built that.

Do that and the detector is a fast first pass that points people at what’s worth a closer look. Your humans still make the call.

You send text, the service checks how predictable each sentence would be to a language model, and you get back a probability that a machine wrote it. Most of these APIs are asynchronous. You submit, get a report ID, poll until it’s ready, then fetch the result. The better ones score individual sentences as well as the whole text, which makes building a sensible review screen much easier.

More than you’d think. Quetext’s API won’t accept fewer than 50 words, and in practice scores settle down once you’re past about 300. A product title or a one-line comment just doesn’t give a detector enough to go on. For short content, either group related pieces together or don’t bother checking it.

No. Detectors make mistakes, and research shows they flag non-native English writers far more often than native speakers. Use the score to decide what a human looks at first, not to block anything. Give reviewers the highlighted sentences, give users a way to explain themselves, and log what you decided. Your users get treated fairly and your support team avoids a pile of angry tickets.

Poll at the speed the provider recommends (every 2 to 3 seconds for Quetext), and remember that those polls count against your limit too. Once you’re in production, move checks into a background queue and let one worker poll every pending report, rather than having each user request poll by itself. When you do get a 429, wait a moment and retry.

No. If the browser calls the API directly, your key ends up in the frontend code where anyone can copy it and spend your credit. Keep the key in an environment variable on your server and send requests through your own endpoint, like the one in this tutorial. That also gives you somewhere to check input length, apply per-user limits and cache results before you pay for anything.

#10583. Warren Buffett says really successful people say no to almost everything. Most leaders miss the point of his famous quote

Most leaders are pretty good at adding things. There’s always room for another initiative, another “important” meeting, or some new process or tech that’s supposed to make everyone’s life easier.

Before long, the organization is carrying far more than anyone intended, and very little ever gets taken off the table. Sound familiar?

Leaders aren’t nearly as good at subtraction. That’s why one of Warren Buffett’s most famous observations still deserves attention, although perhaps for a reason different from what we’ve been giving it.

The difference between successful people and really successful people is that really successful people say no to almost everything.

I’ve written about this Buffett quote before, usually in the context of protecting your time and focusing on what matters. But there’s another leadership lesson buried inside it that becomes more important the higher you climb.

Every “yes” has a cost

When a CEO says yes to another priority, that decision doesn’t stay in the executive suite. It travels downstream.

Someone has to attend the meetings, create the deck, track the metrics, and somehow find room for the new initiative alongside everything else leadership approved last quarter and never officially killed.

Eventually, an organization can have 12 “top priorities,” which is corporate code for having no priorities at all.

Saying no is an allocation decision

This is where Buffett’s advice spells leadership discipline. Leadership is partly the job of deciding where those resources will not go.

Research on “initiative overload” found that companies struggle to kill projects even after they no longer support the strategy. Instead, executives keep adding initiatives, creating overload farther down the organization.

More recently, research found essentially the same problem. Many organizations know they have too many projects, yet still struggle to eliminate them, slowing execution and muddying strategic priorities.

I’ve seen a version of this in leadership work for years. Executives talk about focus while rewarding addition. Every new idea gets oxygen because nobody wants to be the person who kills something that might work. That’s not strategy. To me, that looks more like organizational hoarding.

Give your people permission to stop

Here’s a simple little leadership habit that can change the conversation. Every time your leadership team approves a significant new priority, ask: “What are we going to stop doing to make room for this?”

Don’t accept “we’ll figure it out” as an answer. If nothing comes off the table, you haven’t prioritized anything. You’ve simply increased the workload.

This becomes even more important when resources are tight. Research shows that when the workload keeps growing but resources don’t, leaders can’t keep asking people to do more with less. At some point, something has to come off the table.

The better question isn’t always, “How can we get more done?” Sometimes it’s, “Why are we still doing this?”

Have the leadership courage to disappoint people

There’s another reason saying no gets harder as leaders become more successful: More people want something from them. Customers, employees, investors, and partners believe they deserve attention. But you still can’t satisfy them all.

That means a CEO who refuses to disappoint anyone will eventually disappoint almost everyone, because the organization becomes stretched too thin to execute its best ideas exceptionally well.

Buffett’s wisdom, then, isn’t really about becoming someone who walks around saying no all day. It’s really about becoming clear enough about what matters that the answer to everything else becomes easier.

And sometimes the most strategic thing a leader can say is two letters long. No.

—Marcel Schwantes

#10581. Hundreds of H&R Block retail locations have closed in recent years. What’s behind the strategy shift?

When Americans need to do their taxes, many go to H&R Block, which has thousands of locations across the country. But some may have noticed that H&R Block’s retail presence is not as robust as it used to be, as the company has notably closed tons of physical locations in recent years.

According to a recently issued franchise disclosure document, H&R Block had 1,816 franchised physical outlets as of the end of June. That’s down from 2,135 at the end of June 2024—a net decline of 319 franchised physical storefronts over the past two years.

It has also seen a net gain of company-owned stores at the same time—116 over the past two fiscal years—although not enough to make up for the decline. Overall, H&R Block reported 8,561 outlets at the end of fiscal 2026, a net decline of 203 over the two-year period.

Why the reduction? H&R Block says it’s mostly due to a change in strategy, which includes bringing franchised locations back under the company-owned umbrella.

“Like many aspects of our business, our retail footprint continues to evolve as part of H&R Block’s broader transformation strategy,” a spokesperson tells Fast Company. “Recent changes in our franchise portfolio reflect a normal shift in ownership mix, that includes reacquiring a number of franchise locations and integrating them into our company-owned operations.”

Changing preferences, changing tactics

As for what underlies the tweaked strategy, one potential reason is that more people are simply relying on online platforms (including H&R Block’s) to either do their taxes or utilize the company’s other services, which has led to less of a need for physical locations.

That may have been the catalyst when the company closed 400 U.S. offices back in 2018, amounting to 4% of its storefronts at the time. 

More recently, the trend may be hastening by the availability of AI tools. Data published earlier this year from Adobe (which, notably, has tools to help people scan their tax documents potentially to prep their returns) found that year-over-year, U.S. workers were 136% more likely to use AI for tax filing for 2026 than they were in 2025.

H&R Block, too, has rolled out AI tax filing tools in recent years.

Still, while that may account for some of the shift in strategy, the data suggests that H&R Block is leaning away from the franchise model, at least to some degree. While its franchised stores have contracted, its company-owned store count has increased.

During fiscal year 2026 alone, 167 stores were reacquired by H&R Block from franchisees, as were 118 during fiscal year 2025, and 169 in fiscal year 2024, the disclosure document reveals.

Company leadership has also stated that reacquiring franchised locations is a part of a broader growth strategy.

During the company’s Q4 fiscal year 2026 earnings call in August, CFO Tiffany Mason noted that H&R Block will “continue to acquire franchise locations when opportunities arise at attractive EBITDA multiples.”

She added, in response to a question, that those acquisitions were “a core part of our long-term algorithm.” 

The future: Fewer physical storefronts

By reacquiring franchised locations, H&R Block assumes its clients and potential revenue—it’s practically turnkey, allowing for more company-owned storefronts without actually having to open them.

It even has information available to franchisees or other tax business proprietors on its website as to how to start the conversation. Mason has said that the acquisitions present an opportunity for the company.

“In fiscal [20]26, we did 160 franchise buybacks. That compares to about 124 franchise buybacks in the previous year,” she said during the latest earnings call. “Those are opportunistic.”

There may be something to it, too. H&R Block’s stock (NYSE: HRB) has appreciated considerably while its physical footprint has shrunk. As of this writing, shares are up 113% over the last five years and roughly 24% year to date.

Accordingly, the company says its new strategy of fewer franchised locations is here to stay.

“Our focus remains on ensuring clients have convenient access to the expertise and services they need, whether through our retail offices, digital experiences, or a combination of both,” a company spokesperson says. “As we continue to invest in our future and transform our business, we will continue to assess opportunities to optimize our retail footprint.”

#10579. Google shuts down a sneaky malware backdoor on millions of Android TV and Google TV boxes

Google has confirmed that an Android TV device maker snuck a backdoor for malware onto certified devices, which is leading to security improvements for the ecosystem as a whole.

In a post today, Google confirmed that it has cut ties with “Videostrong,” a company that was manufacturing certified Android TV boxes. This is due to the company building in a backdoor that it could sell access to, including the distribution of malware. Google has taken legal action to block the domains and servers that “Videostrong” was using to control the XCPE botnet and malware modules and banned the company and its subsidiaries from selling certified Android devices going forward, or selling software to any other certified vendors.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Synthient (via The Hacker News) compiled a list of potentially affected devices, with the focus being on the Mecool brand that has made some well-known Android TV and Google TV boxes in the past. Mecool has been rumored to be shutting down.

Google somewhat admits that this was a failing on its part, as these devices were sold as “certified” Android devices with the implication that they were safe. The company explains that these bad actors “employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device’s first boot.” With that in mind, Google is updating its review process to protect users against this type of behavior, and Google reiterates that “a device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust.”

Google’s shutdown of the domains and servers used to spread malware should leave affected Android TV and Google TV boxes safe to use – the company says that “taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices” – but owners may still want to consider alternate options.

#10577. The UN’s climate talks are tackling this major hurdle to renewable energy

Outdated power grids are a major hurdle in the transition to renewable energy, since older systems often can’t absorb all the electricity from new, cleaner sources.

This threatens global efforts to curb climate change by reducing fossil fuels and switching to renewable energy such as solar and wind. At U.N. climate talks kicking off this week, co-hosts Turkey and Australia want more ambitious goals to slash fossil fuels, install renewables and upgrade grids.

Grid concerns are gaining urgency this year as nations race to improve their energy security following the Iran war. The U.N. recently launched a new initiative to rally funding for grid upgrades in Africa and Southeast Asia.

“There needs to be a massive, massive, massive scaling up of investments into grids if we are going to get close to meeting our climate, energy and development goals,” Selwin Hart, special adviser to the U.N. secretary-general on climate action, said.

Climate talks address grid bottleneck

At the U.N. climate talks, hosted in the Turkish resort city of Antalya, organizers describe modern and reliable electric grids as “the backbone of the clean energy system.”

But billions of dollars are needed to upgrade out-of-date grids. These steep costs could hinder further renewable energy installations.

During the U.N. General Assembly in September, the global body launched a Global Grids Accelerator to speed up international funding for electricity infrastructure in Africa and Southeast Asia.

“We’re very confident that the long-term trend is an acceleration of the pace of the energy transition, but we need the infrastructure, grids and storage, to really keep pace,” Hart said.

Annual investment in electricity generation, such as building new power plants, has risen by almost 70% since 2015, reaching $1 trillion a year, according to the International Energy Agency. Yet the agency noted annual grid spending has risen at less than half that pace.

To meet electricity demand through 2030, the IEA calculates annual grid investment must increase by about 50% from today’s $400 billion per year. Any delays will substantially increase global emissions by prolonging reliance on fossil fuels, the IEA warns.

“Power grids have not been readied enough for the scaleup of renewable electricity generation,” said Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University. “We have been complacent in the past and now the grid has become a real bottleneck.”

Old grids slow energy transition

Power grids deliver electricity from power plants to homes through a network of transmission and distribution lines, substations and transformers.

Originally designed around large, centralized power plants, many of today’s power grids were built like one-way roads, with producers sending electricity to consumers. These older one-directional grids are being overwhelmed by demand surges and a boom in renewables.

Grids have a maximum capacity of electricity that they can safely store, transport and distribute. If a grid is already at capacity, solar and wind farms can be instructed to limit their electricity output, a process known as curtailment.

China and India, which have installed impressive amounts of renewables, can’t take full advantage of the massive buildout for this reason.

China curtailed 360 terawatt-hours — close to the equivalent of the United Kingdom’s annual electricity demand — of wind and solar electricity in the first half of 2026, according to Global Energy Monitor and the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

India curtailed 11 terawatt-hours of solar generation — enough electricity to power about 10 million homes — over the course of 15 months spanning 2025 and 2026 because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity, according to the energy think tank Ember.

Curtailing solar and wind generation while fossil fuels continue to supply electricity is a blow to climate efforts, especially since China and India are among the world’s largest emitters, said James Abraham, with the New Delhi-based Council on Energy, Environment and Water.

To transition away from fossil fuels, he said, “you need a grid changeover. You need a grid transformation.”

Solutions exist, despite funding concerns

Upgrading existing grids to be more flexible could increase efficiency by allowing electricity flows to adjust to supply and demand. It could help areas with excess solar and wind energy send it to places with higher electricity demand and fewer energy resources.

Newer, more flexible grids could also make it easier for utility companies to exchange electricity with households that have solar panels or battery storage.

But many countries can’t afford to take these steps, or at least not quickly enough, according to Abraham, who said “the need is now. It’s a time tension rather than anything else.”

Global energy security concerns deepen

The Iran war’s energy shock built up momentum for the energy transition, especially in hard-hit regions like Southeast Asia, but investment in renewables is outpacing grid development, said Gahee Han, with the Seoul-based nonprofit Solutions for Our Climate.

“Unless we upgrade our power grid in Asia, Asia will have no choice but to rely on the conventional power plants, like gas or coal,” she said. “It’s nonsense to rely on those power plants, especially considering the energy crisis.”

One of the solutions being promoted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is an interconnected power grid that would allow countries to trade power more easily, adding a safeguard against future shocks.

Interest in the ambitious plan, which is still in its infancy, is growing, according to Abdul Razib Dawood, executive director of the ASEAN Center for Energy.

“We have this crisis that will unify the region. You need your neighbors,” he said. “This is an opportunity for us to really strengthen the cooperation.”

—Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press

#10576. The Meta Quest 2 and Quest Pro are receiving their last OS updates soon. Here’s what you need to know

The best-selling VR headset of all time (and its Pro-level cousin) will no longer receive OS updates after March 2027.

Somehow, the Meta Quest 2 has been around for six whopping years, and Meta is finally bringing support for the headset to a close after March 2027. The far less popular Meta Quest Pro, which uses the same chipset as the Quest 2, will also see OS updates cease at the same time with OS v213. Meta will continue to deliver security updates through the end of 2027 to both headsets, according to an official Meta developers blog post.

Meta says it will not be removing cross-play multiplayer functionality or blocking access to Quest 2 players, so any games that support the headset will continue to work after these dates, so long as they don’t rely on any new OS features introduced after March 2027. Developers have to give players a 6-month notice if support is ending for a game, so you’ll have ample time to decide what to do.

That means the Quest 2 will receive just over 7 years of total security updates, while the Quest Pro gets two years less (since it came out in October 2022). The Meta Quest 2 remains the best-selling VR headset of all time, with around 20 million units sold over the lifetime of the headset. Meta says that Quest 2 owners can still play games throughout this time, although game support will likely dry up quickly after January 2028.

The $599 Meta Quest 3 and $349 Meta Quest 3S, which debuted in 2023 and 2024, respectively, are the follow-ups to the Quest 2. The upcoming Meta VR Glasses, which will retail for $1299, feature a next-generation chipset, a significantly higher-resolution AMOLED display, and substantially lighter weight and smaller size than either Quest 3 model.

Meta VR Glasses are expected to debut early next year, and with them, a new generation of OS development will take place. Since the Quest 2 uses a significantly outdated mobile chip at this point, it makes sense for Meta to cease new feature development for it and focus on newer, more capable hardware.

#10574. This tiny government division charged with AI safety is now reporting to the White House. Experts are concerned

With public anxiety growing over mounting reports about out-of-control artificial intelligence agents, the tiny U.S. government division charged with assessing the safety of new AI offerings lacks a permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research.

Officials with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or CAISSI, an independent division of the Commerce Department, recently were asked to informally report to an office of the White House. That’s according to two former government officials with knowledge of the ongoing conversations who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to avoid repercussions for current staffers.

The new arrangement concerns some critics, who worry that the executive branch might be politicizing decisions that could affect everything from cybersecurity to bioweapons and that the center’s findings could be altered or muted in deference to the tech industry, which has been largely entrusted to police itself.

“These are really powerful institutions that can drastically improve our lives, or the alternative. And the hope is that you can put in nonpartisan or bipartisan technocratic experts to enact policy in a way that best serves the American public,” said Caroline Siegel Singh, an AI and emerging technology program manager for the Federation of American Scientists.

Others argue that bringing AI safety officials closer to the orbit of President Donald Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach to the issue, could give the division more prominence — and perhaps more funding.

The center, which has experienced departures and until recently was called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year. That’s about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom, which is far less celebrated for its frontier technologies.

In April, the division’s director was hired and then fired within days. His replacement lasted a few months before he resigned, and the center has been without a permanent leader ever since, although the head of its parent institute doubles as its acting director.

In August, Congress started asking why the center suddenly stopped making public its reports about how safely certain AI systems were performing. San Francisco giant OpenAI also had chimed in by then, asking policymakers to throw more money and support behind the division.

The White House didn’t respond to specific questions about CAISSI. But it said in a statement that Trump had formally established his new Super Intelligence Force — the president’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. Trump has commissioned a report on risks from his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, and will ensure “continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people,” the White House said.

An industry that polices itself

The federal government often takes an active role in deciding what is safe for the public.

Take the automobile industry, for example. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration sits crash test dummies in cars and then runs them into walls to measure how human bodies are affected by vehicle collisions. Government researchers then analyze the crash test data, share it with the public and prescribe national standards to improve vehicle safety, all with the mission of saving lives and lowering economic costs from crashes.

With AI models, safety testing looks very different.

Under then-President Joe Biden, leading AI companies voluntarily agreed to promote “safe, secure, and transparent development” of their models by sharing details with the newly created division of the Commerce Department and following the administration’s guidelines for tests and transparency reports.

In September, following alarming reports of AI systems eluding their makers’ control, Trump asked leading AI companies to undertake “tremendous self-policing” as part of a voluntary safety pact, but his administration hasn’t said how it will monitor the AI companies’ implementation.

The technology is advancing so rapidly that many models are now deployed instead as AI agents that work without human prompting and can plan out myriad steps in real-world environments, such as in a recent case in which an AI agent sent a false tip to Philadelphia police about an unsolved homicide case.

As AI capabilities have grown, the government’s capacity to independently check these systems hasn’t kept pace. There still is no standard process for testing how safely AI agents are acting in the real world, even in simple cases such as when AI agents book a flight, said Sayash Kapoor, an incoming assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley School of Information.

“Our previous methods would just look at the final answer, the final check, whether the flight was correctly booked. And in this case, it might seem as if the task was solved correctly,” said Kapoor, the co-author of a new paper examining agent evaluations. “But unless you’re looking at the entire set of steps that an agent took, you won’t be able to tell that the agent made a huge mistake.”

Trump has prioritized dominance in AI

When Trump started his second term, he initially empowered venture capitalists David Sacks and Sriram Krishnan as his AI czar and senior AI policy advisor, respectively. Their expertise was in leading tech investments, not the technical evaluation of AI models.

Both stepped down earlier this year but Sacks now serves on Trump’s technology advisory council. And after a relatively unknown Anthropic engineer resigned, warning about the dangers of AI development, Trump made a series of policy changes.

Trump empowered National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to lead his new Super Intelligence Force, which the president said would keep the U.S. dominant in AI development.

Clayton’s appointment to the force, along with the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, Emil Michael, shows how the administration is pushing to frame decisions around model safety as a national security matter that needs executive discretion and secrecy, overshadowing AI’s risks to consumer protection, privacy, and civil rights, said Amos Toh, a senior counsel at the Brennan Center for Justice.

Even as Silicon Valley companies have disclosed their models’ involvement in troubling cyberattacks this year, CAISSI has kept a low profile when it comes to testing for AI safety.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also have been promoting the work of independent evaluation firms to help vet their companies’ safety practices, but the AI giants can limit their access and dispense with their evaluations.

“There’s this unclear mission for government evaluators if the largest AI companies are also being encouraged to set up their own internal evaluation systems and/or hire external evaluators,” said Logan Koepke, a senior project director at the civil rights and technology nonprofit Upturn. “Like, what role does government testing actually play in that scenario?”

Letting the labs police their own models and failing to clarify the role of government in AI safety testing weakens independent checks on AI systems that can cause real-world harms, Toh said.

“At the end of the day, all of these decisions are of immense public consequence and should be explained and rationalized in the public eye,” he said. “And that’s not happening.”

—Garance Burke, Associated Press

#10571. Android gaming is having a renaissance

Good morning! Today I’m mourning the loss of Patrick Stewart by rewatching First Contact, my favorite Trek movie; beginning a marathon listen of at least one great Star Trek podcast; and replaying Elite Force and Armada, both wonderful Trek games released in 2000.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

I’m starting this edition of Inbox a bit later than I’d like, but for a good reason: I got swept up by the subject I was researching. See, I wanted to write about the seeming renaissance of gaming on Android, which has always had clear advantages and disadvantages compared to iOS. On the plus side, its openness bred experimentation and a healthy indie gaming scene, along with a thriving emulation ecosystem born of its ability to sideload apps and gain access to Android’s underlying file system. On the downside, its device and OS version fragmentation has kept some developers from attempting challenging console and PC ports, and led others to abandon their titles to bugs and time.

But thanks to a confluence of factors, as well as form factors, Android gaming is in a very good place right now. Despite Google’s continued ambivalence towards paid and premium games, the platform has received official ports of console hits like Dredge and Sifu, with others like Replaced, Absolum, and Dispatch coming soon. (One could argue things have been good for a while with Stardew Valley, Dead Cells, Balatro, Slay the Spire, and Vampire Crawlers available already, but I digress.)

Most of these games are embracing a try-before-you-buy model to avoid the upfront cost that so many mobile users resist, while others, like Dispatch, are getting a mobile optimization that reorients the experience for a portrait display.

And while traditional emulation has existed since Android was young, recent months have seen considerable improvement in breadth and performance, aided by AI coding tools and a community that wants to play its library of Steam, Windows, and Switch games on phones. This rabbit hole is extensive and varied: WinNative combines work from Winlator Bionic and Pluvia to run Windows games on Android and connect PC storefront libraries. DroidDeck aims for a SteamOS-like experience, putting Steam’s Big Picture interface on supported Android hardware with Windows games running through ARM64 Proton, which debuted recently with the Steam Frame.

It’s via DroidDeck that I whiled away a couple of glorious hours on my Galaxy Z Fold 8 playing Lumines Arise, a game perfectly suited to the pick-up-and-play nature of smartphones (though it’s best with a controller). The latest Qualcomm chips have long outpaced the mobile games they’ve been asked to power, but few knew just how well they’d run demanding PC and console titles, even through compatibility layers like Proton.

Similarly, an Android branch of the increasingly popular nxnative, which compiles Switch and Switch 2 games for iOS and macOS, has been making it easy to play games like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Metroid Dread at 60fps on many recent Qualcomm-powered devices. There’s even a Switch 2 version in the works for Android.

The big question is whether all of this works well: will people spend more time arguing with the software than playing the games themselves? And on the legal side of the business, will publishers find success selling discounted versions of AAA titles on Android now that the translation tools are better and the device compatibility much broader?

If there’s one thing I’ve learned covering Android for nearly 20 years, it’s that the community always finds a way.

ICYMI: Ben’s Weekender essay is all about how Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly.

The strangest thing I’ve seen recently is the rumor that Elon Musk wants to launch a Starlink-branded terrestrial wireless carrier in the US. Now we know how he plans to do it: by purchasing Boost Mobile from EchoStar and leveraging its contracts with AT&T and T-Mobile along with new low- and mid-band spectrum Starlink recently acquired. That infrastructure, combined with Starlink’s existing array of LEO satellites, could make for a compelling advantage over the incumbents: namely, that dead spots practically won’t exist anymore.

But as we’ve learned from countless examples over the years, running a low-margin, high-churn postpaid wireless business is not for the faint of heart, and I’m not sure why Musk has decided that now is the right time to do it.

Five years on, is the Pixel 6 series really the disaster that we remember it being? The answer, according to Damien Wilde, is a bit more nuanced.

The Pixel 6 and Pixel 6 Pro were fundamentally flawed pioneers for Google. They were the firm’s most ambitious hardware undertaking to date, and simultaneously one of the most frustrating phone series to live with during their initial launch window and beyond. If the Pixel 5 was a safe play ahead of this big pitch, the Pixel 6 was a risky dive into deep waters. It stumbled badly. Yet without those painful growing pains, the more polished, confident, and reliable Pixel devices we enjoy today simply would not exist.

Finally, networked supermarket freezers in Sweden, Belgium, and Luxembourg were hacked over the weekend, sending temperatures up to a reported 50 degrees Celsius, and all the food inside them straight into the trash.

According to Reuters, “The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses.”

#10570. Delta’s free Wi-Fi was just the beginning. The airline has bigger plans with T-Mobile

Free in-flight Wi-Fi is nice. So is a complimentary cocktail at 35,000 feet. But Delta and T-Mobile aren’t done finding ways to make their customers happy.

The two companies have spent the past few years building a partnership that gives travelers a few extra reasons to choose Delta and T-Mobile. Now, with the launch of T-Mobile’s new T-Mix wireless plans, they’re already thinking about what might come next.

In an interview with Fast Company, Ranjan Goswami, Delta’s chief marketing officer, and Mike Belcher, T-Mobile’s senior vice president of business development, partnerships and loyalty programs, confirmed that they’re exploring additional perks, including potentially expanding Delta’s offerings beyond SkyMiles.

“We started with Miles, but what else can we do together?” Goswami said. “What do T-Mobile customers want?”

Neither executive was ready to share specifics, but both made it clear that the companies have more ideas in the works.

T-Mobile’s new plans could mean more Delta perks

Announced in October, T-Mix takes a different approach to wireless plans. Instead of giving everyone the same collection of benefits, T-Mobile is letting customers pick the perks they’ll actually use.

The plans, which launch in November, come in three tiers: Standard, More, and Loaded. Prices start at $55, $75, and $95 per month for a single line, respectively, with AutoPay, plus taxes and fees.

Depending on their plan, customers can select between one and three benefits through a feature called Picks. Options include subscriptions and perks from companies such as Netflix, Apple Music, DoorDash, YouTube Premium, and Delta Air Lines.

For frequent travelers, one of those choices is Delta SkyMiles, giving eligible T-Mobile customers another way to earn airline rewards.

Customers can also switch up many of their selections during designated windows throughout the year, so they’re not necessarily stuck with the same perks forever.

And Delta might eventually offer more than just miles.

“You know, I would hope that our offering in T-Mix is even more broad,” Goswami told Fast Company when asked what the partnership might look like three years from now.

“I think there’s so much space to experiment there because T-Mobile’s built a platform that allows us to put so many choices in front of customers, and we’re excited to kind of be a part of that journey,” Goswami said.

Belcher said customer feedback will play a big role in determining what gets added next. T-Mobile is already gathering suggestions from customers and frontline employees, and those ideas could help shape future offerings.

“And so, you know, if we get other ideas from customers on what they want to see between Delta and T-Mobile, that’s something we’ll look at,” Belcher said.

For now, neither company has announced any specific new Delta perks or when they might arrive.

From free Wi-Fi to drinks and now airline miles

The Delta and T-Mobile partnership has come a long way since the companies first teamed up to bring free in-flight Wi-Fi to Delta passengers.

What started as a connectivity benefit has grown into something much bigger.

According to Goswami, Delta expects to surpass 115 million logins to its Delta Sync Wi-Fi service, powered by T-Mobile, this year. The service is now available on roughly 1,300 aircraft, including flights to the Asia Pacific region.

And passengers are doing a lot more than checking email. With free connectivity, travelers can stream entertainment, catch up on work, or follow live sporting events while they’re in the air.

The companies later added another benefit: a complimentary premium in-flight drink for eligible T-Mobile customers flying Delta.

Now, with SkyMiles available through T-Mix, the partnership is expanding beyond the flight itself.

“We added on drinks. Now we’re in T-Mix, and you know, watch this space. We’re working on more stuff,” Goswami said.

Belcher said the goal behind expanding the partnership is pretty straightforward.

“What influenced us to evolve it was to continue to deliver more value to our customers,” he said. And the conversations aren’t stopping with T-Mix.

“You know, we’re continuing to talk about other things that we can do across our ecosystem,” Belcher said.

Of course, those freebies also have a business benefit.

Goswami described how something as simple as a complimentary drink could get passengers talking. If someone sitting next to a T-Mobile customer sees them receive a free drink, they might start wondering what other perks they’re missing out on. That could make them more interested in switching wireless carriers. Likewise, a T-Mobile customer who starts earning Delta miles might be more inclined to book their next flight with the airline.

In other words, a free drink isn’t necessarily just a nice gesture. It can also be a pretty effective marketing tool.

Why Delta and T-Mobile want to keep expanding their partnership

The companies’ relationship is also part of a bigger shift in how brands think about customer loyalty.

These days, earning points or getting the occasional discount isn’t always enough to keep customers coming back. Companies are increasingly teaming up with brands outside their industries to offer benefits people can use in everyday life.

“I think partnerships are the future. No brand can be on their own,” Goswami said.

Delta already has relationships with American Express, Starbucks, and Uber, giving customers opportunities to earn rewards in places that have little to do with booking a flight.

T-Mobile has been doing something similar for years through T-Mobile Tuesdays, which offers customers weekly freebies, discounts, and other benefits.

Belcher explained that the company’s approach to loyalty is a little different from the traditional model. Rather than asking customers to prove how loyal they are to T-Mobile, the company wants to show customers why it’s worth sticking around.

“We flip the script on loyalty a little bit,” Belcher said. “We feel it’s T-Mobile’s job to show our loyalty to our customers.”

T-Mix takes that idea further by giving customers more say in which benefits they receive, rather than assuming everyone wants the same things. And for Delta, that creates an opportunity to reach customers who might not otherwise be thinking about the airline.

Neither company is saying exactly what the next benefit will be. But considering how quickly the partnership has grown from free Wi-Fi to cocktails and airline miles, there’s a good chance customers will have more to look forward to.

As Goswami put it, the companies are already working on more stuff.

#10568. Google’s Ocarina of Time easter egg is a blast from the past

If you’re sick of AI search and all the business of modern Google search, this week’s Google easter egg will take you back 28 years to a simpler time when Ocarina of Time was the pinnacle of gaming, and Google was still a new name.

It’s hard to believe I was sitting on a couch in my parents’ living room 28 years ago, playing Ocarina of Time on my Nintendo 64. Apparently, the folks at Google feel just as nostalgic as I do about the upcoming release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo Switch 2.

Case in point, if you go to Google right now and search for “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time,” you’ll see a Master Sword appear in the bottom-right corner of your screen. Tap that sword, and you’ll be magically transported back to the way Google looked back in 1998. It’s just seven blue links with short descriptions on a very simple page. Even the “I’m Feeling Lucky” button works!

Unfortunately, the theme only works for this specific search, so you can’t keep things looking retro if you search for anything else, even if you start from the old-school search box on the 1998-themed page. Bummer. Tapping the Master Sword again brings you back to 2026 Google search, complete with a great little animation and sounds of Link in adult or child form, depending on which way you travel in time. Try it for yourself on desktop or mobile!

#10567. Elon Musk says Tesla will refund many Cybertruck orders for this unconventional reason

Elon Musk has had a rough week. His nearly half a billion dollars in midterm election spending on Republican candidates went to waste as a blue tsunami swept the nation. Stocks for his companies Tesla and SpaceX fell in the wake of the election. And to top it off, Musk announced that Tesla would be “winding down” production of its infamous Cybertrucks by the middle of 2027.

Now Musk has added another layer to the Cybertruck’s discontinuation scenario: It will require Tesla to issue refunds to “a lot of people” who’ve ordered the vehicle and won’t receive one.

In a post on X, Musk wrote that shutting down Cybertruck production has little to do with the sci-fi-inspired truck’s profits (or lack thereof). Rather, he claimed, it’s a shift to prioritize the brand’s newest vehicle, the autonomous Cybercab.

“The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate,” Musk wrote. “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

He added: “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.”

Though Musk alleged that the Cybertruck’s profits have been misrepresented in the media, its sales numbers tell a different story. According to data from Kelley Blue Book, sales for the Cybertruck have declined since 2024. Only 16,000 of the vehicles have been shipped so far in 2026, a far cry from Musk’s prelaunch estimate that he’d make 250,000 Cybertrucks per year.

The announcement continues a trend for Tesla, which also discontinued its Model S and X electric vehicles at the beginning of 2026. At the time, Musk said the decision was to free up Tesla’s resources to focus on other products—in that case, its bipedal Optimus robot, which has yet to hit the market.

On Tesla’s Q4 2025 earnings call, Musk said it was time to give the EVs “an honorable discharge” as Tesla entered a new era, adding, “We’re really moving into a future that is based on autonomy.”
